title: The Doctor of Medicine and of Law: Mainz, the Burned Muniment Room, and the Ancestor at the Root of the Jung Line
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Mainz Cathedral, the mob turned back from the Jews
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year in the corpus entry for Bernard of Clairvaux; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Bernard of Clairvaux comes down the Rhine and finds the monk Radulf preaching the crowds against the Jews of Cologne, Mainz, Worms and Speyer. He confronts him at the cathedral, orders him back to his monastery, and the killing in the four cities stops. Five centuries before any Jung is said to practise medicine here, the arch-chancellor's city already holds the shape it will keep: a cathedral, a market, a river, and a population that can be turned in an afternoon and turned back in one.
suggested_refs: The Mainzer Dom, standing through every episode in this journey
sources: bernard_clairvaux.journey.json, stop 'Mainz, the mob against the Jews turned back'

stops.name: Mainz Altstadt, the elector opens a university
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of foundation
stops.campa: Archbishop Adolf II of Nassau founds a studium generale in the Altstadt, a few streets from the Markt and from the presses Gutenberg left behind. It teaches theology, law and medicine, and it stays Catholic through the whole confessional century that follows, its doctors licensed under a prince who is also a bishop and the empire's arch-chancellor. Any physician practising in Mainz with a degree takes it in this house or brings it from another Catholic faculty. The rectorship of this university is the office the Jung tradition will one day claim.
suggested_refs: The Alte Universitat of Mainz, founded 1477, near the Markt
sources: General historical record of the University of Mainz and its confessional character

stops.name: Mainz, Luther writes to the archbishop-elector
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Martin Luther sends a letter to Albert of Brandenburg, Archbishop-Elector of Mainz, enclosing ninety-five theses against the indulgence his archbishop's agents are selling in Saxony. The letter reaches the city; the answer is silence, and then a heresy file forwarded to Rome. Mainz itself does not turn Lutheran. It keeps its elector and its cathedral, so that a hundred years later a physician in these streets is a Catholic physician in a Catholic prince-bishopric, which is the only structural thing anyone can say with confidence about the man this journey follows.
suggested_refs: Luther's covering letter to Albert of Brandenburg, 31 October 1517

stops.name: Mainz, the electorate in the new century
stops.date_confidence: context stop; no event, the year is a marker
stops.campa: The century opens with Mainz as one of the seven electorates of the Holy Roman Empire, its archbishop arch-chancellor for Germany and first voice at an imperial election. The Jesuits hold the schools, the cathedral chapter holds the land, the university licenses the physicians, and the walls hold everything else. Into this city, family memory and three published biographies of Carl Gustav Jung place an ancestor: a doctor named Carl Jung, of whom no two of those accounts give the same date, the same offices, or the same affiliations.
suggested_refs: The Electorate of Mainz in the reign of Johann Adam von Bicken
sources: General historical record of the Electorate of Mainz
Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and His Work
Frank McLynn, Carl Gustav Jung: A Biography (1996)

segments.name: The Physicians of the Rhine and the Main

stops.name: Worms, the city physician's complaint
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication
stops.campa: Philipp Begardi, city physician of Worms, publishes his Index Sanitatis and puts into it a complaint against a traveling healer called Johann Faust, who takes money for cures and is gone before the patients can find him again. It is the oldest kind of document the Rhineland produces about medicine: a licensed man drawing a line against an unlicensed one, in writing, with his office behind him. Mainz lies downstream on the same river. When the Jung tradition claims a doctor of medicine and of law, it is claiming the Begardi side of that line.
suggested_refs: Philipp Begardi, Index Sanitatis, Worms 1539

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Faust book goes to press
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: Johann Spies prints the Historia von D. Johann Fausten at Frankfurt. The scholar who sells himself for knowledge enters the German book trade in the same Rhine and Main country, and nearly the same generation, as the physicians on whom the Jung tradition will later be hung. The Frankfurt fair moves these volumes into every city with a bookseller, Mainz twenty miles upriver among them. The figure of the learned man with a second and hidden discipline is already in the local air before anyone writes down the name of a Dr Jung.
suggested_refs: The Spies Faustbuch, Frankfurt am Main, 1587

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Michael Maier settles
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Michael Maier, physician to the late Emperor Rudolf II, returns from England and settles at Frankfurt, and from here issues his defences of the Rosicrucian Fraternity along with the emblem books that make him the most widely read alchemical author in Germany. Gerardus Dorneus, the Paracelsian, works the same city. Barbara Hannah, three and a half centuries later, will place the Jung ancestor of Mainz thirty kilometres from these two men and in their own decades, and will refuse to claim anything beyond the proximity.
stops.quote: it would be noteworthy - in view of Jung's later great interest in alchemy - if his direct ancestor had been connected with these two famous alchemists.
stops.quote_source: Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and His Work, quoted at carljungdepthpsychologysite.blog
suggested_refs: Maier's Atalanta Fugiens (Oppenheim, 1617) and Symbola Aureae Mensae (Frankfurt, 1617)
sources: Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and His Work

stops.name: Leiden, Fludd answers for the Fraternity
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month approximate and set to place it after Maier in travel order
stops.campa: Robert Fludd, an English physician, publishes at Leiden a short apology for the Rosicrucian brotherhood against its accusers, the second physician within a year to put his own name behind an order nobody can produce a living member of. The manifestos travel out of Kassel and Frankfurt into every Latin-reading household in the empire. Membership in this fraternity is asserted constantly and proved never, which is the evidential shape that the sentence about a Rosicrucian Dr Jung of Mainz will have when it is finally written.
suggested_refs: Robert Fludd, Apologia Compendiaria, Leiden 1616

stops.name: Magdeburg, the alchemist dies and his books do not
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: Maier goes from Frankfurt to Kassel and the landgrave's service, then to Magdeburg, and dies there in the fourth year of the war. He leaves a shelf behind him: Atalanta Fugiens, Symbola Aureae Mensae, reprinted and translated for a century afterwards and still in print in the twentieth. The Mainz physician of the Jung tradition leaves nothing at all. No treatise, no edition, no letter, no manuscript in any catalogue searched for this journey. Barbara Hannah will name him beside Maier three centuries later on the strength of thirty kilometres and a shared decade.
suggested_refs: The posthumous reprint history of Maier's alchemical emblem books

stops.name: Dresden, Boehme lodged with a court physician
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: Jacob Boehme, summoned to Dresden and examined by the electoral doctors, is found not to be a heretic and is lodged two months in the house of a court physician whose name the record does not preserve. The shoemaker of Gorlitz spends that season among men who hold a medical licence and an interest in the things the licence does not cover. The Jung tradition asks for exactly this kind of man at Mainz, and it offers exactly this kind of evidence for him: a figure standing inside somebody else's documented story.
suggested_refs: The Dresden examination of Jacob Boehme, 1624

segments.name: The Doctor of Medicine and of Law

stops.name: Mainz Altstadt, the doctor of two faculties
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undated: Hannah gives only 'the early seventeenth century'; no source supplies a year of birth, matriculation, graduation or arrival, and the year here is a placement, not a claim
stops.campa: Barbara Hannah, writing the psychiatrist's life from what his household told her, puts an evidently learned doctor of medicine and of law named Carl Jung in Mainz in the early seventeenth century. No street is given, no parish, no house, no faculty roll, no year. He holds two doctorates in a city whose university grants both, in a principality whose prince is also its bishop. Every later account of him, in print or on a genealogy page, runs back to this sentence or to one closely resembling it.
stops.quote: an evidently learned doctor of medicine and of law called Carl Jung
stops.quote_source: Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and His Work, quoted at carljungdepthpsychologysite.blog
suggested_refs: Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and His Work (1976), opening pages on ancestry
sources: Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and His Work, quoted at carljungdepthpsychologysite.blog/2021/04/23/early/

stops.name: Mainz, Kircher ordained at the arch-chancellor's seat
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year in the corpus entry for Kircher; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Athanasius Kircher, twenty-six years old, is ordained priest at Mainz, seat of the arch-chancellor of the empire, and stays on in the city reading the mathematical books the Jesuit house keeps. He is walking these streets in the same decade the Jung tradition puts its physician in them. Kircher can be pinned to the year and to the church. The physician cannot be pinned to anything, and the difference between the two men is not learning or standing but which of them belonged to an order that kept its own archive out of reach of artillery.
suggested_refs: The Jesuit house at Mainz, where Kircher was ordained in 1628
sources: kircher.journey.json, stop 'Mainz, ordination to the priesthood'

stops.name: Mainz Altstadt, the rectorship claimed
stops.date_confidence: unattested: the office comes from modern chronologies built on Deirdre Bair, which date the man c. 1650 and give no year for the rectorship; no rectors' list or matriculation register has been seen
stops.campa: The chronologies compiled from Deirdre Bair's biography name the earliest known Jung ancestor as a Catholic physician, lawyer and university rector, and date him about 1650. A rector's name is the one thing a university always writes down. It goes into a list that begins at the foundation and never stops, and it is read out again at the installation of every man who follows him. That no such list at Mainz can be searched for this name is not evidence the office was never held. The lists themselves burn, in this journey, within sixty years.
stops.quote: Dr. Carl Jung (c. 1650), a Catholic physician, lawyer, and university rector
stops.quote_source: Junguipedia, 'Chronobiography of Carl Gustav Jung', drawing on Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (2003)
suggested_refs: The rectors' list of the University of Mainz for the seventeenth century

stops.name: Mainz, Kircher flees the war down the Rhine
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month in the corpus entry for Kircher
stops.campa: In November the Swedish army is coming down the Rhine and the Jesuits scatter ahead of it. Kircher goes out through Mainz and Koblenz and beyond the empire toward Lyon, and never lives in Germany again. A man with a house, a practice and a family in Mainz cannot leave the way a priest with an order behind him leaves. Whatever the physician of the tradition is doing this month, he is doing it in a city about to change hands, and the men who could have written his name into a book are on the road west.
suggested_refs: Kircher's flight route through Mainz and Koblenz, November 1631

stops.name: Mainz, the Swedes take the city
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Gustavus Adolphus enters Mainz two days before Christmas and holds it for four years. The elector is gone, the Jesuit college is turned out, the university empties, and a Lutheran garrison sits in the capital of a Catholic electorate. Contributions are levied, houses are quartered, the sick multiply every winter. A physician who stays through this occupation practises under an authority that will not license him and does not keep his papers, which is one plain reason a whole career of these years can leave nothing behind it.
suggested_refs: The Swedish occupation of Mainz, December 1631 to 1635
sources: General historical record of the Thirty Years War at Mainz

segments.name: The War, the Plague, the Death

stops.name: Mainz, the garrison years
stops.date_confidence: context stop covering the occupation years; no dated event
stops.campa: Typhus and plague travel with the armies up and down the Rhine, and Mainz loses a large share of its people across the war, to disease and to flight alike. Physicians in an occupied city work the way they work in every such year: bleeding, purging, theriac, and burial. The dead are counted by the parish and the parish books go into the town hall. This is the practice the tradition claims for its Dr Jung. No bill, no consilium, no plague ordinance bearing his name has been found anywhere reachable, and the parish books of these years are themselves among the losses.
suggested_refs: Plague ordinances and mortality registers of Rhineland cities in the 1630s
sources: General historical record of the Thirty Years War at Mainz

stops.name: Mainz, the elector returns to a smaller city
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1635/36; the sources differ on the year and it is set here at the later bound
stops.campa: Imperial and Spanish troops take Mainz back from the Swedes, and the archbishop's government comes home to a city holding fewer people than it held at the start of the war. The university reopens slowly. French garrisons will arrive in their turn before the peace of 1648. Through all of it the story the Jungs will tell keeps one figure standing in the same place: a doctor of two faculties, holding an office, in a town sacked, occupied, retaken and half emptied inside his own working lifetime.
suggested_refs: The imperial recapture of Mainz, 1635/36
sources: General historical record of the Thirty Years War at Mainz

stops.name: Mainz, the death in the year 1645
stops.date_confidence: contested: McLynn gives 1645, the Bair-derived chronologies give c. 1650, Hannah gives only the early seventeenth century; no burial register has been seen and the month and day are defaulted
stops.campa: Frank McLynn, opening his life of the psychiatrist with the ancestry, writes the single sentence that carries the whole tradition into print. He gives no archive, no register, no shelfmark, and no year of birth to set against the year of death. Every genealogy page that repeats the date is repeating him, whether or not it names him. The war has three years left to run. The man said to have died in this year leaves no stone, no epitaph, and no entry in any burial book that survives to be opened.
stops.quote: The Jung family came from Mainz, and it is known that there was a Dr Carl Jung who died there in 1645...affiliated to the Rosicrucians.
stops.quote_source: Frank McLynn, Carl Gustav Jung: A Biography (Bantam Press, 1996), ancestry chapter; verified by Internet Archive full-text search of item carlgustavjung00mcly
suggested_refs: Frank McLynn, Carl Gustav Jung: A Biography (1996), first chapter
sources: Frank McLynn, Carl Gustav Jung: A Biography (1996)
Internet Archive / Open Library full-text search, item carlgustavjung00mcly

stops.name: Mainz, the other date
stops.date_confidence: the Bair-derived value, given as c. 1650 and five years after McLynn's; recorded alongside his rather than instead of it
stops.campa: The chronologies built on Bair put the ancestor at about 1650, five years past McLynn's death date, and Hannah puts him only somewhere early in the century. Michael Owen, writing on Jung and the lunar cycles, opens with McLynn's own clause and then describes Hannah's man instead. Four accounts, four positions on a fifty-year line, and no document underneath any of them. Choosing a single point among them would invent the evidence that would justify the choice, so none is chosen here.
stops.quote: The Jung family came from Mainz, and a doctor of medicine and law, called...
stops.quote_source: Michael Owen, Jung and the Native American Moon Cycles; verified by Open Library full-text search
suggested_refs: The Junguipedia chronobiography and its Bair citations
sources: Michael Owen, Jung and the Native American Moon Cycles
Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and His Work

stops.name: Mainz, the French occupy the city
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: In October a French army occupies Mainz almost without a siege, at the opening of the Nine Years War. The elector's court withdraws upriver. Louis XIV's engineers set about the works, and the townspeople of the archbishop's own capital are put to labour on the fortification of a French garrison. The occupation will last less than a year. It ends with an imperial army coming back across the Rhine to take the city, and with artillery working on the town from the far bank through the better part of a summer.
suggested_refs: The French occupation of Mainz, October 1688

stops.name: Mainz, the bombardment and the muniment room
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the end of the siege; the archive loss is attested by Hannah without a date, and she assigns it to the wrong war
stops.campa: The imperial siege ends on the eighth of September with the French marching out and much of the town burned behind them. Barbara Hannah records what this costs the family history in one clause, and misdates it to the War of the Spanish Succession, a decade and a half too late. The fire that fits is this one. Everything a physician of the 1640s would have left in a municipal hand, licence and oath and tax roll and testament and burial entry, is in that building while it burns.
stops.quote: the municipal archives of Mainz were burned in the course of a siege
stops.quote_source: Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and His Work, quoted at carljungdepthpsychologysite.blog
suggested_refs: The 1689 imperial bombardment of Mainz and the destruction of the municipal records
sources: Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and His Work

stops.name: Mainz, the tree that ends at 1688
stops.date_confidence: the 1688 cutoff is stated by the genealogical compilers and by the Junguipedia chronology; Hannah gives no year at all, and the stop year is a marker
stops.campa: The genealogists who work the Jung line say it comes to an abrupt end in 1688 and stop there. From McLynn's 1645 to that wall is forty-three years, not the seventy the compilers sometimes write. What lies beyond the wall is not empty; it is unreadable. The tradition survives the fire because it was carried in mouths and not in muniments. It reaches the twentieth century uncorrected, every paper that could have corrected it having gone into the ash of 1689.
suggested_refs: The 1688 cutoff in the compiled Jung genealogies
sources: Geni.com genealogy profile for the Jung family (JavaScript-rendered, seen only as a search snippet)

stops.name: Mainz, no stone and no book
stops.date_confidence: gap stop; the year is a marker for the state of the evidence, not an event
stops.campa: No tomb, no marker, no epitaph and no parish burial entry for a Dr Carl Jung has been located at Mainz for the 1640s. No treatise, edition, translation or manuscript is attributed to him in any bibliography searched. Maier's books are being reprinted in these very years and Dorn's stand in every alchemical library in Europe. The Mainz Jung has left one sentence inside other men's books and nothing whatever of his own. That is the state of the evidence, not proof that he never lived.
suggested_refs: Stadtarchiv Mainz and the Dom- und Diozesanarchiv Mainz, holders of what survived 1689
sources: Absence of result across Wikipedia, Geni, WikiTree, FamilySearch summaries, and bibliographic search

segments.name: The Line Comes Back Into the Light

stops.name: Mainz, Franz Ignaz Jung practises medicine
stops.date_confidence: attested year of birth (1759-1831 per Wikidata Q108838675); the year of his beginning to practise is not recorded
stops.campa: Franz Ignaz Jung is born at Mainz and becomes a medical practitioner in the city, the first Jung the documents actually hold. He marries Sophie Maria Josepha Ziegler. Between him and the doctor of the tradition lie about a hundred and fifteen years and a burned muniment room, and no source in print or online supplies one link across that gap. The family is still in Mainz and still in medicine, which is either the tradition quietly confirming itself or the exact reason the tradition took the shape it took.
suggested_refs: Franz Ignaz Jung, 1759-1831, Mainz physician

stops.name: Mainz, Goethe at the siege
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year in the corpus entry for Goethe; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Goethe rides with the Prussian army to the siege that takes Mainz back from the Jacobin republic, and when the town falls he pushes into a crowd about to lynch a returning collaborator and gets the man out alive. He is a morning's ride from Frankfurt where he was born, and a century and a half from the physician of the family story. The Jungs will lay claim to Goethe for an entirely different reason within two generations, and the claim will be no better documented than the one about Mainz.
suggested_refs: Goethe's own account of the fall of Mainz, 1793
sources: goethe_full.journey.json, stop 'Mainz, the siege and the mercy to the fleeing'

stops.name: Mannheim, the field hospital
stops.date_confidence: the relocation is attested; the year is inferred from the son's birth at Mannheim in 1795 and is not itself recorded
stops.campa: Franz Ignaz Jung leaves Mainz for Mannheim, some fifty-nine kilometres up the Rhine, to take charge of a field hospital in the wars of the Revolution. The family the tradition roots in the archbishop's city is now in the Palatinate. This move is the whole reason later accounts sometimes say Mannheim where the older story says Mainz. There is no drift in the record and nothing needs reconciling: a Mainz physician relocated for a war, and his son was born on the far side of the move.
suggested_refs: The Mannheim field hospital under Franz Ignaz Jung, 1790s

stops.name: Mannheim, the birth of Karl Gustav Jung
stops.date_confidence: attested as 7 September 1795 in both the English and German Wikipedia articles; Wikidata Q2739430 gives 1794 and Basel, and both of those values are wrong
stops.campa: A son is born to Franz Ignaz and Sophie Ziegler at Mannheim and is named Carl Gustav. He will read medicine, be swept up in the Prussian proceedings against the student fraternities, spend a year in prison at Berlin, and leave Germany for good. The name the family story gives to a doctor at Mainz in the 1600s reappears here, on a boy born in a garrison town in a war year. Between the two the name is carried by nobody the record shows: Franz Ignaz is not a Carl, and this boy's own son will be Johann Paul Achilles.
suggested_refs: Karl Gustav Jung, born Mannheim 7 September 1795

stops.name: Basel, the emigration and the chair
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: Carl Gustav Jung crosses into Switzerland and takes a post at the University of Basel, where he will hold chairs including anatomy, surgery and obstetrics and run the city's medical teaching for four decades. The line the family places in a Catholic prince-bishopric on the Rhine is now settled in a Reformed republic on the same river, and it stays there. Everything in the story after this point is Swiss and documented; everything before it, apart from three generations at Mainz and Mannheim, is tradition.
suggested_refs: The medical faculty of the University of Basel under Karl Gustav Jung

stops.name: Basel, the Rheinsprung and the rectorship
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of installation
stops.campa: Six years after arriving he is installed rector of the university, in the old building above the Rheinsprung where the faculties have met since the fifteenth century. The office the Bair chronologies claim for the ancestor at Mainz is the office his supposed descendant actually holds: in another country, on a recorded date, with his name in a printed list that no army has burned. He is a documented figure in his own right, and the ancestor's story only touches him in passing.
suggested_refs: The Alte Universitat on the Rheinsprung, Basel, seat of the rectorate

stops.name: Basel, the second unprovable ancestry
stops.date_confidence: the currency of the legend is attested; its truth is not, and English Wikipedia calls it likely a legend; the year is a marker for the period the story circulated
stops.campa: A story runs in the family that this Basel professor is the natural son of Goethe. His grandson will tell it at dinner tables for years and then withdraw it, saying only that Sophie Ziegler was a friend of Goethe's niece. The withdrawal itself misplaces her by a generation: Sophie was the professor's mother, so the psychiatrist's great-great-grandmother, and the psychiatrist's actual paternal grandmother was Sophie Frey, third of the professor's three wives. The family carries two unprovable ancestries at once and tells them both.
stops.quote: Jung entertained his contemporaries with the family legend that his paternal grandfather was the illegitimate son of Goethe and his German great-grandmother, Sophie Ziegler. In later life, he pulled back from this tale, saying only that Sophie was a friend of Goethe's niece.
suggested_refs: The Goethe paternity legend in the Jung family, called 'likely a legend' by English Wikipedia

stops.name: Basel, the professor's death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Carl Gustav Jung dies at Basel on the twelfth of June, sixty-eight years old, having been physician, professor and rector, and having founded an institution in the city for children nobody else would teach. He is buried in a town that keeps its registers. His son Johann Paul Achilles goes into the church rather than into medicine and becomes a pastor with a philology degree he never uses. The medical line breaks for exactly one generation, and the name skips that generation with it.
suggested_refs: The grave of Karl Gustav Jung at Basel, died 12 June 1864

stops.name: Kesswil, the name comes back
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: In the parsonage at Kesswil on Lake Constance a son is born to Pastor Johann Paul Achilles Jung and Emilie Preiswerk and is given his grandfather's name. On the mother's side stands Samuel Preiswerk, the Basel Hebraist who held that the dead were present in the room. On the father's side stands a Basel professor, a Mannheim birth, a Mainz practitioner, and behind them, in the family's own telling and in nobody's archive, a doctor of medicine and of law in the arch-chancellor's city.
suggested_refs: The parsonage at Kesswil, Thurgau

stops.name: Kusnacht, the alchemists read as psychology
stops.date_confidence: the alchemical work is attested across the 1920s to the 1950s; the year is a marker for the turn, not a dated event
stops.campa: In the house on the Seestrasse the psychiatrist begins buying sixteenth and seventeenth century alchemical books and reading them as psychology, and the two names that come back most often in his notes are Gerardus Dorneus and Michael Maier. Out of that reading come Psychology and Alchemy and, at the end, Mysterium Coniunctionis. Barbara Hannah is in the circle around him and sees what it implies for the family story: the ancestor she has been told about was working thirty kilometres from those two men, in their own decades.
suggested_refs: Jung's alchemical library at Kusnacht; Psychology and Alchemy (1944); Mysterium Coniunctionis (1955-56)
sources: Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and His Work

stops.name: Kusnacht, the grandson dies without naming him
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Carl Gustav Jung dies at Kusnacht at eighty-five, having spent thirty years among the alchemists of the Rhine and the Main and having never, in any published work, placed his own supposed ancestor among them. The memoir dictated in his last years dwells on the Basel grandfather and on the Goethe rumour, and no passage on a Mainz physician has been found in it. The tradition lives in his household and not in his footnotes, and the silence is left standing rather than filled.
suggested_refs: Memories, Dreams, Reflections, recorded and edited by Aniela Jaffe

stops.name: Zurich, Hannah writes it down carefully
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication
stops.campa: Barbara Hannah publishes Jung: His Life and His Work, and into the opening pages go the learned doctor of medicine and of law at Mainz, the note that the municipal archives burned, and the conditional about Maier and Dorneus. She does not claim the connection. She writes that it would be noteworthy if it were true, and leaves it standing there in the subjunctive. This is the most cautious form the story ever takes, and it is also the earliest form of it that anybody can now sit down and read.
suggested_refs: Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and His Work (Putnam, 1976)
sources: Barbara Hannah, Jung: His Life and His Work, quoted at carljungdepthpsychologysite.blog/2021/04/23/early/

stops.name: London, McLynn hardens the date
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication
stops.campa: Frank McLynn's biography comes out from Bantam Press, and in its first chapter the ancestor acquires a year of death and a fraternity that Hannah never gave him. It is known, McLynn writes, and cites nothing at all. Full-text search of the scanned book returns his page and no other, which settles that the sentence is his rather than a genealogist's. From this page the 1645 and the Rosicrucians pass outward into every family tree on the internet, losing his name on the way.
suggested_refs: Internet Archive item carlgustavjung00mcly, ancestry chapter
sources: Frank McLynn, Carl Gustav Jung: A Biography (Bantam Press, 1996)
Internet Archive / Open Library full-text search

stops.name: New York, Bair and the third version
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication
stops.campa: Deirdre Bair's Jung: A Biography appears, and the compilers who build chronologies out of it produce the third version of the man: Catholic physician, lawyer and university rector, dated about 1650, with the family records before 1688 destroyed. Three published biographers now hold three positions and not one of them prints a shelfmark. The tradition had been carried in books for half a century before the genealogy platforms picked it up, which is the reverse of how its transmission is usually described.
suggested_refs: Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (Little, Brown, 2003)

stops.name: Mainz, the archives asked again
stops.date_confidence: attested: the date of this research pass
stops.campa: The Stadtarchiv Mainz and the Dom- und Diozesanarchiv hold whatever survived 1689, and neither was reached in this pass. No guild roll, matriculation register, rectors' list, testament or burial entry naming a Carl Jung has been produced by anyone. What exists is a family that remembers, three biographers who wrote the memory down differently, a burned muniment room, and a city with nine centuries of continuous documented history behind it. The gap is entered as a gap.
